title: Meeting Jelly Roll Morton in Memphis
summary: He first met Morton in Memphis, worked with him, and may have made one of the first records with him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Remembering Jelly Roll Morton: the man, the band

blocks.x: Uh, is there anything else you could tell us about that one record date? The, uh, two sides that are under your name are made, must have been made about the same day or if you remember if it was the next day, it was pretty close together, I think, according to the number on the record.

Uh, well I think they, they, those were made on one date. On one date, you think? Yeah. That's right. And I would like to, while we're talking about it, I would like to, we'll bring in Jell-A-Roll Morton.
Oh yes, I'd like for you to tell us.

Yeah, well I knew, I first met Jell-A-Roll Morton down in Memphis. And, uh, he came into Memphis as the world's greatest piano player. And I guess I was about to, one of the first to, to hear him. He had a blues, Jell-A-Roll blues. This was after Handy had published his blues. And Jell-A-Roll gave a regular concert for him and I and, uh, a couple of ladies. And that's how I first met Jell-A-Roll. And then I went out on some jobs with him, piano and drums, in Memphis. And then we came, then I came to Chicago and, uh, Jell-A-Roll went back to New Orleans. And, uh, then he came up to Chicago. And I think I made one of the first records with him, uh, Jeanette.
I think Jeanette was going there.
Mr. Jell-A-Lord, I believe is one of you.
And he told me I'm the first drummer to ever play a drum solo on a record. And he said it was with his band, but I don't, I never heard that solo. You don't remember? I don't remember.
